parts.label: Part 3
parts.title: What makes a musical expert?
parts.subtitle: How does someone become expert in music? And is it really possible to have a talent for music?
parts.article:
What makes a musical expert?
 
How does someone become expert in music?
And is it really possible to have a talent for music?
 
(A) Does that class of people acknowledged to be musical experts just have more of the same basic skills we are all endowed with, or do they have a set of abilities — or neural structures — that are totally different from those of the rest of us? Are high levels of musical achievement simply the result of training and practice, or are they based on innate brain structure — what we refer to as talent? Talent can be defined as something that originates in genetic structures and that is identifiable by trained people who can recognize its existence before a person has achieved exceptional levels of performance. The emphasis on early identification means that to investigate it, we study the development of skills in children. It is evident that some children acquire skills more rapidly than others: the age of onset for walking and talking varies widely, even between children in the same household. There may be genetic factors at work, but these are closely linked with other factors — with a presumably environmental component — such as motivation and family dynamics. Similar factors can influence musical development and can mask the contribution of genetics to musical ability.
 
(B) Brain studies, so far, haven't been of much use in sorting out the issues. Gottfried Schlaug at Harvard collected brain scans of individuals with absolute pitch* (AP) and showed that a region in the brain called the planum temporale is larger in these people than in others. This suggests that the planum is involved in AP, but it's not clear if it starts out larger in people who eventually acquire AP, or if the acquisition of AP makes the planum increase in size. Results of research into the areas of the brain involved in skilled motor movement are more conclusive. Studies of violin players have shown that the region of the brain responsible for controlling the movement of the left hand (the hand that requires greater precision in violin playing) increases in size as a result of practice. We do not know yet if the propensity for increase pre-exists in some people and not others.
 
(C) The evidence against talent comes from research on how much training the experts do. Like experts in mathematics, chess, or sports, experts in music require lengthy periods of instruction and practice. In several studies, the very best music students were found to have practised more than twice as much as the others. In another study, students were secretly divided into two groups based on teachers' perceptions of their talent. Several years later, it was found that the students who achieved the highest performance ratings had practised the most, irrespective of which talent group they had been assigned to, suggesting that practice does not merely correlate with achievement, but causes it.
 
(D) Anders Ericsson, at Florida State University, approaches the topic of musical expertise as a general problem in cognitive psychology. He takes as a starting point the assumption that there are certain issues involved in becoming an expert at anything; that we can learn about musical expertise by studying expert chess players, athletes, artists, mathematicians, as well as the musicians themselves. The emerging picture from such studies is that ten thousand hours of practice is required to achieve the level of mastery associated with being a world-class expert — in anything. In study after study, of composers, ice-skaters, concert pianists, chess players and master criminals, this number comes up again and again. Someone would do this amount of practice if they practised, for example, roughly 20 hours a week for ten years. Of course, this does not address why some people do not seem to get anywhere when they practise, and why some people get more out of their practice sessions than others. But no-one has yet found a case in which true world-class expertise was accomplished in less time. It seems that it takes the brain this long to assimilate all that it needs to know to achieve true mastery. The ten-thousand-hour theory is consistent with what we know about how the brain learns. Learning requires the assimilation and consolidation of information in neural tissue. The more experiences we have with something, the stronger the memory/learning trace for that experience becomes. Although people differ in how long it takes them to consolidate information neurally, it remains true that increased practice leads to a greater number of neural traces, which create stronger memory representation.
 
(E) The classic rebuttal to this theory goes something like this: What about Mozart? I hear that he composed his first symphony at the age of four! First, there is a factual error here: Mozart did not write it until he was eight. Still, this is unusual, to say the least. However, this early work received little acclaim and was not performed very often. In fact, the only reason we know about it is because the child who wrote it grew up to become Mozart. And Mozart had an expert teacher in his father, who was renowned as a teacher of musicians all over Europe. We do not know how much Mozart practised, but if he started at age two and worked thirty-two hours a week (quite possible, given that his father was a stern task master) he would have made his ten thousand hours by the time he composed his first symphony. This does not mean that there are no genetic factors involved in Mozart's greatness, but that inborn traits may not be the only cause.

questions.question: In the first paragraph, the writer suggests that a talented musician is someone

analyses.content: 原文把“talent”定义为源于“genetic structures（基因结构）”，即先天的生理差异，而非简单的“技能更多样”（排除D）或“意识到自己与众不同”（排除A）。
(Paragraph A) "...or do they have a set of abilities — or neural structures — that are totally different from those of the rest of us? ...what we refer to as talent?"
题目问第一段作者暗示有天赋的音乐家是怎样的人。原文A段第一句提出疑问：他们是拥有和我们一样的技能，还是拥有一套“totally different（完全不同）”的“neural structures（神经结构）”——即我们所说的天赋？并在后文讨论了这种先天的神经结构。对应选项 B（大脑结构与常人不同）。

questions.question: According to the writer, what is unclear about the findings of Gottfried Schlaug?

analyses.content: 题目问关于Gottfried Schlaug的发现有什么不清楚的地方。原文B段提到，虽然拥有绝对音感（AP）的人大脑颞平面（planum temporale）较大，但“it's not clear if it starts out larger... or if the acquisition of AP makes the planum increase（不清楚是本来就大，还是习得AP导致变大）”，即因果关系不明，选 C。
关键词 “cause or an effect” 对应原文的 “starts out larger... or... makes... increase”。
(Paragraph B) "...but it's not clear if it starts out larger in people who eventually acquire AP, or if the acquisition of AP makes the planum increase in size."

questions.question: According to the writer, what has been established by studies of violin players?

analyses.content: 题目问关于小提琴手的研究确立了什么。原文B段后半部分说研究表明，负责控制左手运动的大脑区域“increases in size as a result of practice（因练习而增大）”，即练习后大脑发生了变化，选 A。
“Changes may occur in the brain” 对应 “increases in size”，“following violin practice” 对应 “as a result of practice”。
(Paragraph B) "Studies of violin players have shown that the region... increases in size as a result of practice."

questions.question: According to the writer, findings on the amount of practice done by expert musicians suggest that

analyses.content: “Little to do with” 意味着关联性小，原文通过“practice... causes it（练习导致成就）”而非天赋，支持了这一点。
题目问关于专家音乐家练习量的发现表明了什么。原文C段提到，表现最好的学生练习最多，“irrespective of which talent group they had been assigned to（无论他们被分在哪个天赋组）”，暗示练习是主因，天赋与成就（expertise）关系不大，选 A。
(Paragraph C) "...students who achieved the highest performance ratings had practised the most, irrespective of which talent group..."

questions.question: Anders Ericsson's work with cognitive psychology has influenced other researchers.

analyses.content: 题目说Anders Ericsson在认知心理学方面的工作影响了其他研究人员。原文D段虽然介绍了Ericsson的观点和研究方法，但并未提及他是否“influenced other researchers”，信息缺失，选 NOT GIVEN。
不要因为他很出名就默认他影响了别人，雅思阅读只看文章是否提及。

questions.question: Different areas of expertise seem to have one specific thing in common.

analyses.content: 题目说不同领域的专长似乎有一个共同点。原文D段提到在作曲家、滑冰者等的研究中，“this number (10,000 hours) comes up again and again（这个数字一次又一次出现）”，即共同点是一万小时练习，选 YES。
“Different areas” 对应 “composers, ice-skaters...”，“one specific thing in common” 对应 “this number... again and again”。
(Paragraph D) "In study after study... this number comes up again and again."

questions.question: In order to be useful, practice must be carried out regularly every day.

analyses.content: 题目说为了有效，练习必须每天定期进行。原文D段只举例说“roughly 20 hours a week for ten years（每周约20小时）”，并没有规定必须“every day（每天）”，选 NOT GIVEN。
“每周20小时”不等于“每天都练”，也许周末休息呢？切勿过度推断。
(Paragraph D) "...if they practised, for example, roughly 20 hours a week for ten years."

questions.question: Anyone who practises for long enough can reach the level of a world-class expert.

analyses.content: “Anyone” 过于绝对，原文承认了有人练习了也没用。
(Paragraph D) "...why some people do not seem to get anywhere when they practise..."
题目说任何练习足够长时间的人都能达到世界级专家的水平。原文D段明确指出：“this does not address why some people do not seem to get anywhere when they practise（这解释不了为什么有些人练习了却似乎毫无进展）”，即并非人人都能成功，选 NO。

questions.question: Occasionally, someone can become an expert at a global level with fewer than 10,000 hours' practice.

analyses.content: 题目说偶尔有人能在少于10,000小时练习的情况下成为全球级专家。原文D段说：“no-one has yet found a case in which true world-class expertise was accomplished in less time（还没人发现过少于这个时间就成功的案例）”，选 NO。
“Occasionally” 与 “no-one has yet found a case” 矛盾。
(Paragraph D) "But no-one has yet found a case in which true world-class expertise was accomplished in less time."

questions.question: Existing knowledge of learning and cognitive skills supports the importance of practice.

analyses.content: 题目说现有的关于学习和认知技能的知识支持练习的重要性。原文D段末尾说一万小时理论与我们对大脑如何学习的认知“is consistent with（是一致的）”，并解释了练习如何增强神经痕迹，选 YES。
“Supports” 对应 “is consistent with”。
(Paragraph D) "The ten-thousand-hour theory is consistent with what we know about how the brain learns..."

groups.contentHtml:
Mozart
The case of Mozart could be quoted as evidence against the 10,000-hour practice theory. However, the writer points out that the young Mozart received a lot of from his father, and that the symphony he wrote at the age of was not and may be of only academic interest. The case therefore supports the view that expertise is not solely the result of characteristics.

analyses.content: (Paragraph E) "And Mozart had an expert teacher in his father..."
题目说莫扎特从父亲那里接受了大量的____。原文E段提到莫扎特的父亲是“expert teacher（专家级教师）”，这意味着他接受了大量的“tuition（教学/指导）”，选 E。
题目空格需要名词，“teacher” 对应选项中的 “tuition”。
题目说他在____岁写的交响曲。原文E段纠正传言说：“Mozart did not write it until he was eight（直到八岁才写）”，选 D。
需填数字，原文明确否定了“four（四岁）”，确认是“eight”。
(Paragraph E) "...Mozart did not write it until he was eight."
题目说这部交响曲并不____。原文E段说这部早期作品“received little acclaim and was not performed very often（几乎没获得赞誉，也不常被演奏）”，即不流行，选 A。
“Not performed very often” 和 “little acclaim” 对应 “not popular”。
(Paragraph E) "However, this early work received little acclaim and was not performed very often."
题目说案例支持这一观点：专长不仅仅是____特征的结果。原文E段末尾说这并不意味着没有基因因素，而是说“inborn traits（先天特质）”可能不是唯一原因，选 G。
“Characteristics” 对应 “traits”，“inherited” 对应 “inborn/genetic”。
(Paragraph E) "...but that inborn traits may not be the only cause."
